cards.title: Frostbite: A new CPU architecture discovered, designed and verified by AI

depth.text: someone used AI to design **Frostbite**, a CPU that spreads **independent work** across tiles

Its programs use **interaction nets**: connected graph pieces rewrite locally, and each value has one owner. Architect Labs reports **4.59x performance-per-watt** across 25 workloads against an in-order CPU; commenters question the **baseline and novelty**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some praise AI for making an exploratory chip project more feasible; skeptics say the architecture echoes earlier work and the CPU comparison is too limited.

comments.text: Wow, I posted this and come back a few hours later, and the comments are... a bit depressing honestly. Do people here know what interaction nets are? They are a fundamentally different programming paradigm, different from the most basic harvard architecture of the 1940s. Whether you think this particular implementation will genuinely support them, and whether that will bring the performance they…

I am interested to have end products with really good UX driven by peak performance and optimizations which blows my mind because it’s so well perfected as humans weren’t part of its process. As of now, I don’t see any of that being the goals even let alone the result. Instead what I see is that everyone is in a race to have as much product out as possible by the same standards that applied to…

The title is a bit misleading—humans came up with all the insights and innovations here. What AI has done, which it is exceptionally good at, is take decades of brilliant ideas buried in research literature and synthesize them into a coherently engineered product. It would seem that AI is now doing an end-run around the innovator’s dilemma, or at least part of it, by dramatically lowering the R&D…

I'm quite skeptical; their baseline is a in-order CPU, instead of a modern out-of-order design, and they're testing a small amount of programs. Also, I'm not an expert in CPUs, but the underlying idea doesn't seem entirely novel - WaveScalar explored dataflow-based architecture 20+ years ago.

Isn’t this similar to every other alternative architecture that it relies on a “sufficiently smart” compiler to handle the all the dependencies and get increased efficiencies. It isn’t clear to me what exactly is different this time and why it will work better in practice than all the prior attempts.

cards.title: If you can't explain something in simple terms, you don't understand it (2017)

depth.text: a story uses **Feynman’s teaching** to argue that **simple explanations** can show you **understand an idea**

Feynman tried to prepare a **freshman lecture** on why spin one-half particles obey **Fermi-Dirac statistics**, but couldn't; he said that meant “we don’t really understand it.” The comments push back: audience, communication skill, and **learner effort** also matter.

cards.camps: Two camps: some see simple explanations as evidence of understanding; others say communication skill, audience, and learner effort matter too.

comments.text: I think this idea is often misunderstood and used as an excuse by people who don’t want to make any effort to understand a complex concept and want to blame the results of their laziness on the explanation or the explainer. There are things where you may be given an explanation in simple terms, but the concept requires effort on the part of the recipient of the explanation to really understand…

The article is just a bunch of quotes from Richard Feynman and John Gruber. There is little insight and I even think the article is misrepresenting the quotes. Feynman said "if you can't explain it on a freshmen level ". Leaving out that qualifier distorts the statement. The other quote about the magnets is also overly reductive. Saying "I don't understand it in terms you're more familiar with"…

Explain to what level? E.g some topics common here. How do you explain NP in simple terms? "Things that are hard to compute?" That's simple, but not much of an explanation. It leaves the listener with a practically useless definition. And how do you explain even something practical as Heartbleed or Rowhammer? Etc. And then there's another barrier, of course: the audience. You may use simple…

Whenever I see this I think to myself, “I can explain something in simple terms, but it will take more time than you have.” Or in other words, “simple” does not imply ”short.” However I’ve seen a lack of appreciation of this distinction play out in some exec meetings where “clarity” is prioritized above nuance. There is definitely great skill involved in crafting a message for an audience, and…

I don’t think this is true because it makes an assumption that reductionism is always possible, you can always distill every increasingly complexity into something less and less complex and maintain the overall behavior. I don’t think complexity is always reducible because sometimes the detailed nuance is absolutely critical to the distinction. You may be able to take core ideas from something…

cards.title: PostgreSQL 19

depth.text: PostgreSQL adds **easier table cleanup**, **more replication features**, and a bunch of performance and monitoring improvements

The release adds **REPACK**, which replaces VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER; its **CONCURRENTLY** option rebuilds tables without access-exclusive locking. It also adds **sequence replication** and a WAIT command so standbys can wait for log positions to be written, flushed, or replayed.

cards.camps: Two camps: some praise the features as exciting; others worry companies haven't adopted earlier releases and don't want feature creep in a database.

comments.text: Amazing release, really exciting features: - REPACK CONCURRENTLY to reclaim disk space, which also affects performance. - Logical replication of sequences - Fantastic addition. This is a missing piece in the major-version upgrade story which required extra scripting, and enable additional usecases. - WAIT FOR LSN is a game-changer for read-replicas. For read-after-write, where the write goes to…

Huge respect to Postgres folks, and the features are amazing. But an apologetic opinion: Postgres 18 was released in Sep 2025, and it's just Nov 2026. Half the companies I know haven't even updated to pg17 yet, let alone pg18's async I/O or anything. There are already so many features that are unadopted and unproven at scale. IMHO the last software that I want to see feature creep or a large…

> Change JIT to be disabled by default (Jelte Fennema-Nio) That was long overdue. The performance impact on perfectly fine tuned queries was horrendous. It's also disabled by most OSM apps that make heavy use of PostGIS for exactly that reason. Maybe it wouldn't be that bad if a copy-and-patch kind of JIT would be used?
A huge thank you to all contributors for this gift

cards.title: Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations

depth.text: someone posted a paper and formal proofs about **finite-time blow-up** in the **Navier–Stokes equations**

The repository includes the **79-page paper** and a Lean formalization, but **no data**. The certificate isn't in the repository; the paper says it will be released, and a rigorous computation checking its conditions is outside the formalization and repository.

comments.text: Isn’t it a little nuts that this is only the second-biggest result of the day? This is the unforced version of the problem. OpenAI found an example that uses a carefully designed external force to break the equations, so this one is more "realistic" in a sense.
